body.text: Inside the two unofficial lobby groups spending big on the Victorian election
In short
Two groups have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads ahead of the Victorian election.
The ads have been viewed more than 39 million times and focus on key election issues such as policing, potholes and debt.
Transparency activists say voters have a right to know who is trying to influence elections.
Two unofficial lobby groups have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on social media ads ahead of the Victorian election, with their membership and sources of funding remaining hidden.
ABC NEWS Verify can reveal that Better Victoria spent up to $355,000 on Facebook and Instagram ads while FixVictoria spent up to $262,000.
Combined, the two groups spent more money on ads than the official account for Victorian Labor between August 26 and November 26, according to Meta.
A FixVictoria campaign insider said its total budget was closer to roughly $2 million.

Better Victoria's ads focus on issues such as potholes and the management of infrastructure projects, while FixVictoria's ads often feature short AI video depictions of what they describe as the state's "tsunami of debt" represented by flood water.
Both groups' ads appear sympathetic to the Liberal Party's position.
Collectively, they have been viewed more than 37 million times across Instagram and Facebook.

Ads from the groups have also run across Google's ad network. A Google spokesperson said the company reviewed the ads and determined they were not subject to its election policy as they did not mention a party, candidate or office holder.
Meta did not respond to questions around funding and transparency.
A Victorian election law loophole means that because the ads are promoting issues rather than specific candidates or a party, the advertisers are not required to disclose who is funding them.
New ads, old hands
FixVictoria and its AI-generated ads may be new, but the brains behind it are not new to politics.
The public face is Gideon Rozner, a former Liberal staffer and former policy director of conservative think tank the Institute of Public Affairs (IPA).
FixVictoria is run by former IPA executive Deborah Henderson.
It is understood the organisation has roughly 30–60 members, mostly individuals, who remain unidentified.
Mr Rozner told ABC NEWS Verify the group was a private membership organisation and insisted it was not backing a specific party.
"FixVictoria is a strictly non-partisan organisation," he said.
A spokesperson for the Victorian Liberal Party said it did not "direct or control their activities, advertising or membership".
Mr Rozner said government debt was "terrifying" and the number one issue for the group.

Election marketing veteran Toby Ralph has run more than 50 election campaigns globally including all of John Howard's federal election campaigns and said he had been hired to make the ads for FixVictoria.
"Debt is boring, I mean really boring", Mr Ralph said.
"You need to dramatise it or people fall asleep."
Mr Ralph also insisted FixVictoria was non-partisan.
"We assiduously avoided any contact with politicians".
"If [Ben] Carroll came up with a solid plan for debt, we'd be cheering."
FixVictoria's ads ran on social media until September 30, the day before the VEC's official election period began and ushered in stricter advertising rules.
Better Victoria
The ownership and funding behind Better Victoria is also undisclosed, with just a single name linked to the unofficial lobby group.
Ron Holzer, a lawyer from Caulfield North in Melbourne, is listed as the secretary on official documents.
Mr Holzer said he only held an administrative role and would not speak to the ABC, instead directing questions to an anonymous spokesperson from Better Victoria.
That anonymous spokesperson told ABC NEWS Verify in a written statement that the group had no relationship with any political party and that its funding came entirely from its members.
Better Victoria advertised on Google as well as Meta with Sydney-based advertising agency Bench Media managing these ads.
Bench Media would not answer questions about whether Better Victoria was a client.
Better Victoria continued to run ads into the official election period, something its spokesperson said was within the law.
Victoria's election law loophole
The VEC said it would not comment on specific matters, but that it was monitoring for compliance with the law.
According to the commission, political expenditure is "narrowly defined", and "producing and distributing content does not, by itself, make an entity a third-party campaigner".
This means disclosure of ownership and funding is not legally required.
Clancy Moore, the chief executive of Transparency International Australia, said voters should know who was influencing their elections.
"We need to fix the loophole around third-party campaigners who campaign on issues but not blatantly for or against a party," he said.
"Voters absolutely have a right to know who's behind blatantly political advertising, where they're getting the money from, and whose interests they're representing."
FixVictoria is already planning for after the state election and is considering pressuring the elected government on stamp duty and revitalising Melbourne's hospitality economy.
"No matter what happens on Saturday, FixVictoria's work will continue," Mr Rozner said.
